question.text: This president, the first one from the Democratic Party, sought to destroy the Second Bank of the United States by vetoing its recharter bill.
question.clue: His first term was marred by the Nullification Crisis, which led to the resignation of his first Vice President, John C. Calhoun.

swap.leadin: Answer the following about the early years of the American republic.
swap.text: This rebellion, led by an eponymous Revolutionary War veteran in Western Massachusetts, highlighted the weaknesses of the Articles of Confederation.
swap.clue: This event ended with a capture at Petersham, and it included the defense of the Springfield Armory by Benjamin Lincoln.

question.leadin: Answer these questions about a certain political party in American history.
question.text: Name this party, led by Alexander Hamilton, that opposed the Democratic-Republicans.
question.clue: The Coodies were a faction of this party from Maryland.

swap.leadin: Identify the following Secretaries of State.
swap.text: This politician from Massachusetts was also a successful orator and lawyer; he signed a treaty with Ashburton to resolve a border dispute in Maine with Canada as Secretary of State for William Henry Harrison and John Tyler.
swap.clue: This man debated with South Carolina's Robert Hayne over the issue of nullification.

question.leadin: Answer the following about a supreme court chief justice.
question.text: This man was the first Chief Justice of the United States. He later retired from the position to become the governor of New York.
question.clue: This man became ill after writing Federalist Papers 2 through 5, leading Madison and Hamilton to write all the rest, save one.

swap.text: One major event at the beginning of Van Buren's term was this financial crisis brought on by the abolition of the Second Bank of the United States.
swap.clue: During this event, the Deposit Act transferred precious metals away from coastal banks, and the Divorce Bill created sub-treasuries.

question.text: Horace Greeley urged "Go West, young man" as an expression of this belief. This almost-rhyming two-word phrase describes the inevitability of the U.S. expanding all the way across North America.
question.clue: This concept was first proposed in the Democratic Review by John O'Sullivan, who used it to argue for the annexation of Texas.

swap.text: This 1818 treaty signed during the tenure of Monroe saw the almost complete demilitarization of the Lake Champlain and Great Lakes areas.
swap.clue: The Webster-Ashburton treaty built on this 1818 agreement which curtailed the use of naval boats on the Great Lakes and set much of the US-Canada border at the 49th parallel.

question.leadin: Identify the following about the Magna Carta's legacy in American history.
question.text: In this man's Braintree Instructions, he argued that the Stamp Act was "directly repugnant to the Great Charter itself." He served as the second President of the United States.
question.clue: This man quipped that "facts are stubborn things" while defending Thomas Preston for his role in the Boston Massacre.

swap.text: This president, who essentially failed to respond to Dorr's Rebellion, is also famous for rebelling against the Whigs after succeeding William Henry Harrison.
swap.clue: His Secretary of State was one of the few to remain loyal to him, possibly because he was negotiating an end to the Aroostook War.

question.leadin: This woman met her long-lost brother Cameahwait during the event she is most associated with.
question.text: Name this Shoshone woman who, along with her husband Toussaint Charbonneau and son Pompey, accompanied one expedition after meeting them in the lands of the Mandan and Hidatsa tribes.
question.clue: After a group of explorers identified Cameahwait as this figure's long-lost brother, he gifted horses to those explorers.

swap.leadin: This man's son was killed by future Civil War general Daniel Sickles.
swap.text: Name this man who watched the bombardment of Fort McHenry and later combined his writing with a British folk tune.
swap.clue: This man prosecuted the would-be assassin of Andrew Jackson, Richard Lawrence, who was committed to an insane asylum for the rest of his life.

question.leadin: Answer these questions about controversy over American neutrality between Jeffersonians and Hamiltonians.
question.text: This man sparked an international incident when he asked for a suspension of American neutrality in support of France. George Washington granted this [emphasize] "Citizen" asylum after he arrived in Philadelphia.
question.clue: This man's attempt to raise a militia for the invasion of Spanish Florida nearly led George Washington to deport him.

swap.leadin: Members of this group were targeted by the Edmunds-Tucker Act, which also disincorporated their Perpetual Emigration Fund.
swap.text: Name this group whose members committed the Mountain Meadows Massacre. One member of this group was subject of the case Reynolds v. United States.
swap.answerHtml: Mormons [or Latter-Day Saints; or members of the LDS Church; or members of the Church of the Latter-Day Saints]
swap.clue: This group was forced to flee from a town called Nauvoo after their leader was killed by a mob in nearby Carthage, Illinois.

question.text: This President of Texas was responsible for moving the Texas archives to Austin. This successor of Sam Houston authorized "redbank" currency, which further exacerbated Texas's debt.

swap.leadin: Answer some things about money in the United States.
swap.text: In order to prevent state governors from having authority to forgive debts, Hamilton pushed for this clause to be included in the Constitution. It also prohibits states from making treaties and was used as the basis of Fletcher vs. Peck.
swap.clue: The Supreme Court rejected the petitioners' argument that the creation of the Warren Bridge was in violation of this clause of the Constitution. This clause was also the basis for the decision in Fletcher v. Peck.

question.text: This member of the Kitchen Cabinet, once referred to as the "Whig of the west," staunchly supported the Maysville Road veto. He edited the United States Telegraph from 1825 to 1836, which served as an official mouthpiece for the Jackson administration.

swap.leadin: This faction, which officially called itself as the Equal Rights Party, opposed a standard system of weights and measures and called for abolition of the Electoral College.
swap.text: Name this faction of Jacksonian Democrats, who got their more common name from the matches they used at their first meeting.
swap.clue: This group, which advocated specie circulation, was originally called the Equal Rights Party and formed when William Leggett was thrown out of Tammany Hall.

question.text: A Seneca Falls resident at the time of the convention, this woman attended it and was inspired to start her own feminist publication, The Lily, which promoted reformed fashion advice and temperance.
question.clue: This reformer published the first newspaper edited entirely by women, the temperance journal The Lily.

swap.leadin: Identify the following relating to a battle FTPE.
swap.text: This Kentucky colonel claimed to have killed Tecumseh at the Thames. For his insistence that he did so, he was elected Vice-President in 1837. He is also famous for living openly with a female slave and their mulatto children.
swap.clue: During one election, this politician used a slogan that began with the chant "rumpsey dumpsey, rumpsey dumpsey," even though John Catron wrote that "a lucky random shot" did not qualify him for his post.
